O R I E N TAT I O N
How to use this coursebook
This is a working book, not a book of answers to memorise. Read with a
pencil in hand, test ideas, write down conjectures, and return to your
reasoning when it needs repair.
The course is arranged in four parts. Each
part gathers chapters that share a way of
thinking: comparing quantities; generalising
with symbols; describing space and
measurement; and making decisions from
uncertainty and data. The chapters build on
one another, but each is also designed to be
entered on its own after the prerequisite
check.
Every chapter follows the same inquiry
rhythm. You meet a situation that
mathematics can clarify. You frame a
question. You build the concepts and
representations needed to answer it. You
practise until the method is reliable. Then
you investigate, communicate, apply and
reflect. The answer key at the back supports
this cycle; it should confirm your reasoning,
not replace it.

COURSE DEVELOPS

H OW T H E L A B E L S WO R K
Definition boxes state the precise meaning of a term. Key idea boxes connect a method
to a bigger principle. Common error boxes show a mistake worth anticipating. ATL
boxes make a learning skill explicit and give you a way to practise it. Criterion strips
name the MYP criterion and strands being developed.
AT L · U S I N G T H E A N S W E R K E Y W E L L
Attempt the question fully before
checking. If your answer differs, locate
the first line where your reasoning
diverges. Mark the correction in a
different colour and write one
sentence explaining why the
alternative was wrong. That sentence
is often more valuable than the correct
number.
ACA D E M I C H O N E S T Y
Copying a solution without
understanding it creates the
appearance of progress and hides a
gap. Use sample answers to compare
methods, not to replace your attempt.
In investigations, report your own data
and reasoning, and acknowledge any
source you use.

T H E P R O G R A M M E I N P R A C T I C E
The MYP framework in this
course
The Middle Years Programme asks students to learn mathematics as a
connected, conceptual and applicable discipline. This course is designed
around that expectation: concepts organise the content, contexts give it
purpose, and criteria make the quality of thinking visible.
The aims of MYP mathematics
The MYP mathematics framework sets out to help students enjoy mathematics, develop
curiosity, build conceptual understanding, apply mathematics to real situations, communicate
reasoning, think critically and creatively, and appreciate the international and historical
dimensions of the subject. In Year 2, this means strengthening the bridge between informal
reasoning from earlier years and the more formal symbolic work that follows.
K E Y C O N C E P T 0 1
Form
The shape, structure
and organisation of
mathematical objects:
how a ratio is written,
how a graph is arranged,
how an expression is
built. Form helps us
notice what is
mathematically the
same beneath different
appearances.
K E Y C O N C E P T 0 2
Logic
The reasoning that
connects claims to
conclusions. Logic asks
not only “Is it true?” but
“How do we know, and
for which cases?” It is
the discipline behind
justification,
generalisation and
proof.
K E Y C O N C E P T 0 3
Relationships
Connections between
quantities, variables,
representations and
ideas. A ratio, a linear
pattern, a proportional
graph and a rate are
different ways of
expressing
relationships.
Related concepts used in this course
EQUIVALENCE
Different forms with the same
value or meaning.
JUSTIFICATION
Reasons and evidence that
support a claim.
MODELS
Simplified representations of a
real situation.
PATTERNS
Regular structure that repeats or
grows predictably.
QUANTITY
Number, magnitude, measure
and unit.
REPRESENTATION
Words, symbols, tables,
diagrams, graphs.
SIMPLIFICATION
Rewriting without changing
value or meaning.
SPACE
Position, shape, direction and
dimension.
SYSTEMS
Related parts working under
shared rules.

A S S E S S M E N T
Knowing, investigating,
communicating, applying
MYP mathematics is assessed against four equally weighted criteria.
Each is marked out of 8, giving a total out of 32. Every chapter in this
book identifies the strands it develops and provides at least one task
designed for criterion-based feedback.
What Year 2 looks like in practice
By Year 2, students should be moving from
recognising a method to selecting it. A
student working securely at this level can
choose a representation, carry a multi-step
procedure accurately, explain why the steps
A
KNOWING AND UNDERSTANDING
i. Select appropriate mathematics when
solving problems in familiar and
unfamiliar situations.
ii. Apply the selected mathematics
successfully when solving problems.
iii. Solve problems correctly in a variety
of contexts.
B
INVESTIGATING PATTERNS
i. Apply mathematical problem-solving
techniques to recognise patterns.
ii. Describe patterns as relationships or
general rules consistent with correct
findings.
iii. Verify whether the pattern works for
other examples.
C
COMMUNICATING
i. Use appropriate mathematical
language, notation, symbols and
terminology in oral and written
explanations.
ii. Use different forms of mathematical
representation to present information.
iii. Communicate coherent mathematical
lines of reasoning.
iv. Organise information using a logical
structure.
D
APPLYING MATHEMATICS IN REAL-LIFE
CONTEXTS
i. Identify relevant elements of authentic
real-life situations.
ii. Select appropriate mathematical
strategies when solving authentic real-
life situations.
iii. Apply the selected strategies
successfully to reach a solution.
iv. Justify the degree of accuracy of a
solution.
v. Justify whether a solution makes sense
in the context of the authentic real-life
situation.

sensible. In unfamiliar contexts, they may

Criterion B is not only “spot the pattern”.
Students need to test cases, express the
relationship in words or symbols, and test
the general rule against further examples,
including a case that could have broken it.
Criterion C values clarity: correct notation,
labelled diagrams and a logical order.
Criterion D requires attention to units,
accuracy and meaning—not just calculation.
LEVEL
TYPICAL EVIDENCE IN THIS COURSE
1–2

support to start; communication is
fragmented.
3–4

explanation is partial.

accurately in familiar and some
unfamiliar tasks; justifies most steps.
7–8
Works independently and flexibly;
verifies generalisations;
communicates precise, coherent
reasoning and evaluates accuracy
and meaning.
These are summarised, course-specific descriptions to help students recognise progress. They are not
official IB level descriptors and must not be used as a substitute for the current subject guide.
ATL skills in mathematics
Approaches to learning are the deliberate
habits that make inquiry possible. This book
integrates them where they do real work:
organising a solution, testing a conjecture,
choosing a representation, reading a data set
critically, or collaborating on a fair
experiment.
Criterion tasks
Criterion tasks are longer than routine
practice. They are marked against named
strands, so the goal is not only the answer.
You are judged against the descriptors, not
ranked on a curve: two students can take
different valid routes and both reach high
levels. A strong response typically:
Communication — notation, diagrams,
labelled axes, clear explanations.
Critical thinking — counterexamples, error
analysis, evaluating claims.
Research — finding and judging data,
naming sources.
Collaboration — sharing methods, dividing
a task, reaching agreement with evidence.
Organisation — planning an investigation,
managing data and units.
Reflection — judging the quality of a
solution and setting a next step.

transformations. The sequence is an
independent design, not an official or
compulsory MYP order.

RATIO AS COMPARISON
A ratio is not a pair of numbers that happen to sit beside each other. It is a statement
about how quantities are related by multiplication, and the order of the statement is
part of its meaning.
There are three common ways to write a two-part ratio: in words, with a colon, or as a fraction.
A ratio of 3 parts blue to 5 parts yellow can be written “3 to 5”, 
, or  when the fraction is
understood as a comparison, not as a share of the whole. The notation you choose should make
the meaning clearer, not merely shorter.

SIMPLIFICATION
Two ratios are equivalent when they describe the same multiplicative relationship. The
numbers may change; the comparison does not.
Multiplying or dividing both terms by the same non-zero number produces an equivalent ratio.
This is the same operation that produces equivalent fractions, applied to each part of the
comparison. A ratio is in simplest form when the terms are whole numbers with no common
factor greater than 1.

REPRESENTATION
A ratio table organises equivalent pairs so that the scaling factor becomes visible. A
double number line does the same thing spatially; a graph turns the same relationship
into a line.
BUILDING A RATIO TABLE
Each row or column of a ratio table contains one pair of equivalent quantities. To move from
one entry to the next, multiply or divide both quantities by the same factor. A useful strategy is
to scale through a convenient unit, such as one part, because that makes every other entry
easier to find.

 What is a rate?
CRITERION A · I, II

QUANTITY
A rate compares two quantities measured in different units. The comparison becomes a
unit rate when the second quantity is reduced to one unit, so that every rate can be read
as “this much for each one of those”.
Rates are ratios with a difference: the two quantities measure different things. “240 km to 4
hours” compares distance with time, so it is a rate; “4 hours to 2 hours” compares times, so it is
a ratio. Both can be simplified, but only a rate carries two different units.

KEY AND RELATED CONCEPTS
Relationships. An expression links an input
variable to an output: change  and the cost
 changes with it. An equation states the
input for which two relationships give the same
output.
Pattern. Algebraic notation records structure: a
coefficient counts equal variable parts, and a
constant marks a fixed part of the relationship.
Equivalence. Simplifying, expanding and
factorising change an expression's appearance,
not its value; solving preserves equality by
treating both sides alike.

Scientific and technical innovation.

methods. Cost rules, formulas and
spreadsheets are models built from
variables and operations.

orders can each be described by an
expression; choosing between them
requires equivalent forms or a solved

A solution of an equation is a value of the variable that makes the equation true. To solve
an equation, apply inverse operations to both sides until the variable is alone. Addition
and subtraction are inverse operations; multiplication and division are inverse
operations. An equation has the same solutions when the same operation is applied to
both sides.

2. Collect the variable terms on one side and the constants on the other, using inverse
operations on both sides.
3. Divide by the coefficient of the variable.
4. Check by substituting the solution into the original equation: both sides must be equal.

KEY AND RELATED CONCEPTS
Logic. A pattern is not yet a rule. Moving from
several cases to a general claim requires a
reason that covers every case; a single
counterexample is enough to reject a false
claim.
Pattern. Constant first differences produce
linear sequences. A growing staircase behaves
differently: its differences increase, so its rule
has a different structure.
Generalisation. The nth term, a function
machine and a graph are three representations
of one relationship. Each can answer different
questions about the same rule.
GLOBAL CONTEXT AND EXPLORATION
Personal and cultural expression.
Exploration: artistry, craft, creation,
beauty. Repeat patterns in textiles, tiling
and lantern displays are designed with
counting rules that makers must predict
before they cut materials.
A border with a growing number of tiles
and an arch with a growing number of
lanterns both require a general rule: a
maker cannot build every size in order to
count it.

ATL · CRITICAL THINKING IN ACTION
Look for structure before looking for a formula. Compare consecutive terms, then test the proposed
rule at the first and last known positions. A rule that works for two terms may fail at the third; a
counterexample is decisive, while agreement is only evidence.

A term-to-term rule says how to step from one term to the next: “add 2” or “multiply by

AT L · C R I T I CA L T H I N K I N G
Ask what would prove you wrong. Before trusting a pattern, look for a case that could
break it. For a proposed nth term, test the first term and the last known term; for a
claimed general rule, try zero, a negative input or a fractional one. A single
counterexample ends a conjecture, but no number of matching examples is a proof. The
explanation must come from the structure of the rule.

Form. A solid is described by its faces, edges

Measurement. Surface area is counted in
square units, volume in cubic units; capacity
connects the two to litres and millilitres.

D E F I N I T I O N · S O L I D S A N D T H E I R F E AT U R E S
A solid is a three-dimensional shape. Its flat surfaces are faces; a face meets another face
along an edge; three or more edges meet at a vertex. A polyhedron is a solid whose faces
are all polygons.
A prism has the same polygonal cross-section along its length, so its two end faces are
identical and parallel. A pyramid has a polygonal base and triangular faces that meet at
an apex. A cylinder has two parallel circular faces and one curved surface.
A net is a flat pattern that folds to make a solid. The surface area of a solid is the total
area of its faces, measured in square units.

K E Y I D E A · F R O M N E T TO S U R FAC E A R E A
A net must contain every face exactly once, with no gaps and no overlaps. Folding the net
joins some edges, but it does not change any area. Therefore the surface area of a solid
equals the total area of its net. For a prism, this means two identical bases plus the
rectangles that wrap around them.

curved face, two circular edges and no vertices. When counting edges, do not count the

once; a cube net with five squares, or with two squares covering the same position,
cannot close.

D E F I N I T I O N · R E F L E C T I O N
A reflection maps every point to an image on the opposite side of a mirror line, so that
the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the point to its
image. A reflection preserves lengths and angles but reverses orientation, so the image is
congruent to the object.
A shape has line symmetry if a mirror line divides it into two halves that coincide when
folded. That line is an axis of symmetry.

KEY AND RELATED CONCEPTS
Logic. Probability reasons from a defined set of
possible outcomes to a numerical measure of
uncertainty. Its conclusions are only as reliable
as the assumptions behind the model.
Change. Relative frequency changes from one
set of trials to the next, yet it tends to settle as
the number of trials increases.
Models. A sample space and a simulation are
models. Comparing a model with data shows
whether the model is useful, incomplete or
wrong.
GLOBAL CONTEXT AND EXPLORATION
Scientific and technical innovation.
Exploration: mathematical models and
simulations. Forecasters, engineers,
insurers and medical researchers use
probability models to plan under
uncertainty.
A simulation replaces a costly or slow real
process with many rapid random trials. Its
predictions are only trustworthy when the
model captures the important features of
the real situation.

essential?
ATL · CRITICAL THINKING IN ACTION
Before calculating, state the assumptions: are all outcomes equally likely, are trials independent,
and is the sample space complete? After calculating, ask what would change if an assumption
failed. A probability is an argument, not just a number.

include staffing or arrival-rate data, so a longer
audit would make the recommendation more
reliable.”
Marking guidance A: correct ordering, totals,
averages, quartiles and fences. C: clear tables
and box plots with a common scale, correct
units and a coherent comparison. D: a justified
staffing recommendation that uses centre and
spread, acknowledges overlap and states
limitations. For full D credit, the
recommendation must follow from the
evidence and consider the consequence of the
choice.

Glossary
Definitions are written for this course. Where a word has a technical meaning, the definition names
the quantities involved and the context in which the term is used.
absolute value — the distance of a
number from zero; never negative.
alternate angles — equal angles on
opposite sides of a transversal
between parallel lines.
area — the surface enclosed by a
two-dimensional shape, in square
units.
balance method — solve an
equation by applying the same
operation to both sides.
best buy — the product with the
lowest unit price.
bias — a systematic tendency to
favour some outcomes or groups.
box plot — a five-number summary
drawn on a number line.
centre of enlargement — the fixed
point from which enlargement
distances are multiplied.
circumference — the distance
around a circle.
coefficient — the number
multiplying a variable in a term.
common difference — the constant
change between consecutive terms
of a linear sequence.
complement — all outcomes not in
a given event.
composite solid — a solid formed
by joining or removing simpler
solids.
constant — a quantity with a fixed
value.
coordinates — an ordered pair
locating a point on a grid.
corresponding angles — equal
angles in matching positions at
parallel lines.
density — mass per unit volume.
dependent variable — the output
that responds to the independent
variable.
diameter — the distance across a
circle through its centre.
distribution — the pattern of a data
set: centre, spread and shape.
dot plot — values marked by dots
above a number line.
double number line — parallel
number lines showing equivalent
ratios.
enlargement — a transformation
multiplying distances from a centre
by a scale factor.
equation — a statement that two
expressions are equal.
equivalent expressions —
expressions equal for every
permitted variable value.
equivalent ratios — ratios
describing the same comparison.
evaluate — substitute values and
calculate a result.
event — a set of outcomes from a
sample space.
expected count — trials multiplied
by the probability of success.
experimental probability — the
relative frequency observed in an
experiment.
expression — numbers, variables
and operations without an equals
sign.
fair game — a game in which every
player has the same chance of
winning.
five-number summary —
minimum, lower quartile, median,
upper quartile and maximum.
flow rate — the volume passing a
point per unit time.
frequency — the number of times a
value occurs.
function machine — a rule turning
an input into an output.
generalisation — a statement
describing a pattern for all its
terms.
independent variable — the input
that is chosen or changed.
integers — the whole numbers and
their negatives, including zero.
interquartile range — upper
quartile minus lower quartile; the
middle-half spread.
inverse operation — an operation
that undoes another.
like terms — terms with identical
variables and powers.
linear equation — an equation
whose variables have exponent 1.
linear sequence — a sequence with
a constant difference.
line of symmetry — a line that
reflects a figure onto itself.
mean — the sum of the values
divided by their number.
median — the middle value of
ordered data.
mode — the most frequent value.
mutually exclusive — events that
cannot occur together.
net — a flat pattern that folds into a
solid.
nth term — an expression giving
any term from its position .
order of operations — brackets,
indices, multiplication and
division, then addition and
subtraction.
origin — the point 
.
outcome — a single possible result
of an experiment.
outlier — a value far outside the
rest of the data.
parallel lines — lines in the same
plane that never meet.
parallelogram — a quadrilateral
with two pairs of parallel sides.
perimeter — the distance around a
two-dimensional shape.
pi — circumference divided by
diameter of a circle, approximately
3.14159.
polygon — a closed plane figure
made of straight sides.
prism — a solid with constant cross-
section and parallel congruent
bases.
probability — a number from 0 to 1
measuring likelihood.
proportion — an equation stating
that two ratios are equal.
proportional — describing
quantities whose ratio remains
constant.
quadrilateral — a polygon with
four sides.
quartile — a value dividing ordered
data into quarters.
radius — the distance from a
circle’s centre to its circumference.
range — the maximum value minus
the minimum value.
rate — a comparison of quantities
with different units.
ratio — a comparison of quantities
of the same kind.
reflection — a transformation
flipping a figure across a mirror
line.
relative frequency — successes
divided by trials.
rotation — a transformation
turning a figure about a centre.
rotational symmetry — a figure
maps onto itself after a rotation
under 
.
sample — a subset of a population
used for information.
sample space — all possible
outcomes of an experiment.
